newsitem.title: USA: Funds that invest by the numbers.
newsitem.headline: Funds that invest by the numbers.

text.p: Would you rather let a person or a computer run your mutual fund? Increasingly, that's a question investors must answer when they assemble a portfolio of funds.

Most of us are familiar with star fund managers like Michael Price of Mutual Discovery or Shelby Davis of Davis New York Venture. They have earned fame and fortune by spending their time investigating the earnings prospects of individual companies.

They talk to people, look over financial reports and generally try to find out all they can about a company before investing in its shares. Often, their decisions are based on a well-informed gut feeling about a company's future prospects and the real value of its stock.

By contrast, a growing breed of fund managers ignores gut feelings in favour of computerized systems. For example, the management team at Barr Rosenberg U.S. Small Cap (800-447-3332; $2,500 minimum investment; no load) doesn't spend its time visiting companies or trying to get a feel for their prospects.

Instead, the team uses an elaborate system of computer models to decide which stocks the fund should own. That approach has lead the fund to a stellar 20.9 percent annual return during the past five years, vs. 13.7 percent for its typical small-cap competitor.
So-called "quantitative funds" such as Barr Rosenberg U.S. Small Cap have become increasingly popular the past few years.

But do they work? A recent study by the No-Load Fund Analyst, a newsletter in Orinda, Calif., found that quantitative funds are a mixed bag, but do include a couple of worthy candidates for investment.

The funds are relatively new, as a group. The No-Load Fund Analyst identified 26 of them, but only four have been around since before 1990 -- and only two have 10-year records. That said, their methods do offer some potential advantages over the old-fashioned strategies of traditional stock pickers.

For starters, a quantitative system prevents managers from making bets based on instincts or emotion -- the kind of seat-of-the-pants approach that can get funds into trouble. Quantitative funds also have the advantage of consistency, at least as long as their managers continue to use the same computer models to pick investments.

On the other hand, such models can be wrong. For example, a model may tell a fund's manager to sell stocks of companies in a certain industry when the shares trade at historically high prices. But if that industry has unprecedented growth prospects, the old numbers ma no longer apply.
And some numbers can be misleading. Accounting gimmicks can beef up a firm's reported profits, and a quantitative fund manager might not look behind those figures to evaluate the company's prospects.

The upshot? Fund managers who rely on quantitative models have to be every bit as careful as traditional stock pickers. They can't simply rely on numbers. Instead, they must constantly evaluate the effectiveness of their computer models -- making sure that they are up-to-date and that the data can be trusted.

That said, such models can serve as valuable tools for assembling a fund portfolio that will outperform most of its peers. The No-Load Fund Analyst found that four of nine quantitative funds or managers with at least five-year records have outpaced their benchmarks since inception after adjusting for risk.
Barr Rosenberg was one; and the fund is a solid choice for investors who want to put some money in small company shares.
Another standout was John Bogle Jr.

Son of the former Vanguard Chairman, Bogle put together a strong record managing private accounts and Vanguard's Quantitative Numeric fund. Since June 1996, he has managed NI Growth (800-686-3742; $3,000 minimum; no load). Unlike many quantitative fund managers, Bogle is willing to make relatively large bets on particular sectors of the market. As a result, the fund may be somewhat more volatile than its peers.
(EDITORS: Clint Willis is a freelance writer who covers mutual funds for Reuters. Any opinions in the column are solely those of Mr. Willis.)
